formal_name: Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus for Purposes of Educational Assessment and Instruction
description: The Delphi Report is the single most influential consensus document in the critical thinking field. Via a two-year Delphi process involving 46 experts across disciplines, Facione produced both a canonical definition and a detailed skill/disposition taxonomy that has shaped CT assessment instruments (including the CCTST and CCTDI) ever since.
canonical_definition: We understand critical thinking to be purposeful, self-regulatory judgment which results in interpretation, analysis, evaluation, and inference, as well as explanation of the evidential, conceptual, methodological, criteriological, or contextual considerations upon which that judgment is based.

ideal_critical_thinker_profile.description: The Delphi report generated the most detailed portrait of the 'ideal critical thinker' in the CT literature.
social_dimension: reasonable in the selection of criteria
persistent in seeking results as precise as the subject and the circumstances require

six_core_skills.definition: To comprehend and express the meaning or significance of a wide variety of experiences, situations, data, events, judgments, conventions, beliefs, rules, procedures, or criteria.

sub_skills.name: Categorization
sub_skills.description: Identifying the kind of claim, argument, or situation; assigning it to an appropriate category

sub_skills.name: Decoding Significance
sub_skills.description: Detecting the intended meaning behind statements, symbolic expressions, or behavioral data; understanding what something means in context

sub_skills.name: Clarifying Meaning
sub_skills.description: Removing ambiguity; specifying how a term is being used; unpacking the meaning of a complex statement

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 1 (Felt Difficulty) and Phase 2 (Intellectualization) — naming and framing the problem.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Information, Concepts, and Question-at-Issue elements

six_core_skills.definition: To identify the intended and actual inferential relationships among statements, questions, concepts, descriptions, or other forms of representation intended to express beliefs, judgments, experiences, reasons, information, or opinions.

sub_skills.name: Examining Ideas
sub_skills.description: Identifying the role ideas play in an argument; identifying similarities and differences among claims and questions

sub_skills.name: Detecting Arguments
sub_skills.description: Recognizing whether a passage contains an argument or merely assertions; identifying unstated conclusions

sub_skills.name: Analyzing Arguments
sub_skills.description: Identifying the stated and unstated premises; mapping the inferential structure; identifying the pattern of reasoning

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 3 (Hypothesis Formation) — structuring the elements of inquiry.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Information, Assumptions, and Inference elements

six_core_skills.definition: To assess the credibility of statements or other representations which are accounts or descriptions of a person's perception, experience, situation, judgment, belief, or opinion; and to assess the logical strength of the actual or intended inferential relationships among statements, questions, descriptions, or other forms of representation.

sub_skills.name: Assessing Claims
sub_skills.description: Judging whether a statement is credible; evaluating the reliability of sources and evidence

sub_skills.name: Assessing Arguments
sub_skills.description: Judging whether the logical form of the argument is valid; whether the premises are acceptable; whether the premises are relevant and sufficient to support the conclusion

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 5 (Testing) — evaluating whether the hypothesis holds up to scrutiny.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Intellectual Standards application across all elements

six_core_skills.definition: To identify and secure elements needed to draw reasonable conclusions; to form conjectures and hypotheses; to consider relevant information and to draw out the implications carried by data, statements, principles, evidence, judgments, beliefs, opinions, concepts, descriptions, questions, or other forms of representation.

sub_skills.name: Querying Evidence
sub_skills.description: Identifying the appropriate type of evidence needed; questioning the adequacy of available evidence; designing ways to gather relevant evidence

sub_skills.name: Conjecturing Alternatives
sub_skills.description: Forming multiple plausible hypotheses about what explains the evidence; generating rival hypotheses rather than accepting the first

sub_skills.name: Drawing Conclusions
sub_skills.description: Identifying the best-supported conclusion; recognizing when evidence is insufficient for a strong conclusion; drawing probabilistic rather than categorical conclusions when appropriate

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 4 (Reasoning) — drawing out the implications of hypotheses.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Interpretation/Inference and Implications/Consequences elements

six_core_skills.definition: To state and to justify that reasoning in terms of the evidential, conceptual, methodological, criteriological, and contextual considerations upon which one's results were based; and to present one's reasoning in the form of cogent arguments.

sub_skills.name: Stating Results
sub_skills.description: Accurately describing the conclusion reached; clearly articulating what one believes and why

sub_skills.name: Justifying Procedures
sub_skills.description: Explaining why particular methods, criteria, or conceptual frameworks were used in the inquiry

sub_skills.name: Presenting Arguments
sub_skills.description: Constructing well-formed arguments; anticipating objections; organizing reasoning for communication to others

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Corresponds to Dewey's Phase 5 (Testing) and the communicative dimension of reflection.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Purpose, Point of View, and all elements as they are communicated to others

six_core_skills.definition: Self-consciously to monitor one's cognitive activities, the elements used in those activities, and the results educed, particularly by applying skills in analysis, and evaluation to one's own inferential judgments with a view toward questioning, confirming, validating, or correcting either one's reasoning or one's results.

sub_skills.name: Self-Examination
sub_skills.description: Reflecting on one's own beliefs, values, and reasoning processes; identifying one's own biases; asking whether one's own reasoning meets the standards one applies to others

sub_skills.name: Self-Correction
sub_skills.description: Revising conclusions when new evidence warrants; correcting reasoning errors when identified; updating beliefs in light of good arguments

six_core_skills.dewey_connection: Maps to Dewey's metacognitive dimension — the reflective awareness that supervises all phases of inquiry.
six_core_skills.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Intellectual Traits/Virtues, particularly Intellectual Humility and the ongoing application of standards
six_core_skills.special_note: Self-regulation is described as the 'master skill' — it is the skill that makes all other skills function as critical thinking rather than mere analytical competency.

cctdi_dispositions.name: California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory
cctdi_dispositions.description: The dispositional component of the Delphi consensus, developed into a psychometric instrument. Measures 7 traits independently, recognizing that someone can be skilled but not disposed, or disposed but not skilled.

seven_dispositions.description: Eagerness to seek the best knowledge even if that knowledge challenges one's preconceptions or comfortable beliefs
Tolerance of divergent views; sensitivity to the possibility of one's own bias
behavioral_markers: seeks out perspectives that challenge one's own

seven_dispositions.description: Prizing the application of reasoning and the use of evidence even for problems that present difficulty
behavioral_markers: uses evidence to approach complex problems

seven_dispositions.description: Valuing organization, focus, and diligence in inquiry
behavioral_markers: pursues inquiry with order and thoroughness

seven_dispositions.description: Trusting one's own reasoning processes and the conclusions reached through fair application of CT
behavioral_markers: leads others in inquiry when appropriate
makes decisions based on one's own reasoning
defends well-reasoned conclusions under social pressure

seven_dispositions.description: Intellectual curiosity — valuing acquiring knowledge and learning for its own sake
behavioral_markers: curious about wide range of topics

seven_dispositions.description: Prudent judgment; awareness that multiple perspectives are valid; understanding that sometimes conclusions must be reached despite uncertainty
behavioral_markers: accepts uncertainty as the condition of inquiry
applies appropriate epistemic standards to different domains
makes decisions despite incomplete information when required

skill_disposition_interaction.key_insight: Delphi explicitly distinguishes CT skills (cognitive) from CT dispositions (affective). A person may have the skills but not be disposed to use them, or be disposed but lack the skills. The ideal critical thinker exhibits both.

interaction_matrix.high_skills_high_dispositions: Master critical thinker — uses skills readily and accurately
interaction_matrix.high_skills_low_dispositions: Skilled but intellectually undisciplined — capable but unmotivated
interaction_matrix.low_skills_high_dispositions: Well-intentioned but ineffective — motivated but unable to execute
interaction_matrix.low_skills_low_dispositions: Uncritical thinker — neither capacity nor inclination

app_usage.exercise_feature: 6 core skills as exercise categories — each skill generates distinct exercise types
app_usage.progress_tracking: Skills map cleanly to learner progress metrics
app_usage.template_feature: Explanation sub-skills as template for written reflections (Stating Results, Justifying Procedures, Presenting Arguments)

historical_origin.commission_and_purpose: The Delphi Project was commissioned by the American Philosophical Association's Committee on Pre-College Philosophy in 1987 and completed in 1990. The APA recognized that despite decades of CT instruction and assessment in higher education, the field lacked a shared, expert-validated definition of critical thinking — different researchers, educators, and assessment designers were measuring different things under the same label. The project's charge was to produce a consensus definition and framework rigorous enough to ground valid assessment instruments and defensible curriculum design.
historical_origin.methodology: Peter Facione, a philosopher and measurement theorist at Santa Clara University, served as principal investigator. The Delphi method — a structured process for achieving expert consensus through multiple rounds of anonymous feedback, revision, and re-evaluation — was used to avoid the dominance of any single theoretical perspective. Forty-six experts across philosophy, cognitive psychology, education, and social sciences participated over two years. The final report represents genuine multi-disciplinary consensus rather than a single school's view.
historical_origin.scope_and_significance: The resulting report, formally titled 'Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus for Purposes of Educational Assessment and Instruction,' became the most widely cited foundational document in CT education. Its canonical definition — 'purposeful, self-regulatory judgment' — achieved the definitional consensus the commission sought. More importantly, the six-skill taxonomy (Interpretation, Analysis, Evaluation, Inference, Explanation, Self-Regulation) and seven-disposition inventory became the standard framework against which subsequent CT assessment instruments were validated.
historical_origin.lasting_influence: The Delphi Report directly produced or significantly shaped: the California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST), the California Critical Thinking Dispositions Inventory (CCTDI), the Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal's subsequent revisions, and dozens of CT curriculum frameworks in higher education. Its influence is present in virtually every serious CT assessment instrument developed since 1990.

teaching_applications.overview: The Delphi framework's six skills provide a complete taxonomy of the cognitive capacities that CT education should develop. Each skill suggests distinct pedagogical activities that cannot substitute for each other — developing evaluation skill does not automatically develop inference skill, and vice versa.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Ambiguity Audit: present students with a brief text containing three deliberately ambiguous terms or claims. Task: identify each ambiguity, specify the multiple plausible meanings, and explain what would change about the argument depending on which meaning is operative.
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students who skip interpretation and proceed directly to evaluation are evaluating their own interpretation of the claim rather than the author's intended claim — a systematic error that produces confident but misdirected analysis.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Argument Mapping: take a 500-word argument text and produce a visual map showing the conclusion, each stated premise, and the inferential connections between them. Identify every unstated premise that must be assumed for the argument to work.
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students who can identify stated premises often miss the unstated ones — which frequently do more argumentative work than the stated premises and are more vulnerable to challenge.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Evidence Quality Audit: present a set of five claims of varying evidential support quality. Students rank them from most to least well-supported and justify the ranking, citing specific features of the evidence (source reliability, sample quality, design validity, etc.).
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students conflate agreement with credibility — rating claims they agree with as better supported and claims they disagree with as less supported, regardless of the actual evidence.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Alternative Hypothesis Generation: present a set of data and one proposed explanation. Students must generate three additional explanations that could account for the same data, evaluate which is most supported, and specify what additional evidence would distinguish between them.
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students accept the first plausible explanation rather than generating alternatives. This is the reasoning failure behind nearly all confirmation bias effects.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Reasoning Transcript: after completing any analytical task, students write a structured account of their reasoning using the three explanation sub-skills: (1) stating their conclusion clearly, (2) justifying why their method was appropriate for the task, and (3) presenting the argument in a form that anticipates the strongest objections.
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students state conclusions without justifying procedures and present arguments without anticipating objections — producing conclusions that cannot be evaluated by others.

skill_specific_activities.activity: Bias Hunt: after completing an analysis, students go back through their reasoning and explicitly look for instances where their own values, prior beliefs, or motivated reasoning may have influenced which evidence they emphasized, which alternatives they considered, and how they evaluated competing claims.
skill_specific_activities.common_failure: Students treat self-regulation as a formality — confirming that their reasoning was sound rather than genuinely examining it. Self-regulation requires the truth-seeking disposition to be effective; without it, it becomes a rationalizing ritual.

disposition_cultivation_in_instruction.description: The seven Delphi dispositions are cultivated through the intellectual culture of instruction, not through separate lessons. Each disposition implies specific environmental conditions.
conditions: Truth-Seeking requires intellectual environments where being wrong and updating is visibly rewarded rather than penalized.
Inquisitiveness requires freedom to pursue questions beyond the assigned scope and regular modeling of authentic intellectual curiosity by instructors.
Systematicity requires tasks complex enough to reward organized, persistent inquiry over quick approximation.
Maturity of Judgment requires repeated exposure to genuinely uncertain, complex problems where premature closure demonstrably leads to poor outcomes.

six_skills_self_assessment: Interpretation: When I encounter a complex text or argument, do I spend adequate time clarifying its meaning before evaluating it? Can I state, in my own words, what the author is claiming?
Analysis: Can I identify not just the stated premises but the unstated assumptions an argument requires? Have I examined what must be taken on faith for this reasoning to work?

Evaluation: Am I assessing the quality of evidence and argument structure independently of whether I agree with the conclusion? Would I rate this evidence as strong if it supported the opposite conclusion?
Inference: Have I generated more than one possible explanation for the evidence I am examining, or did I accept the first plausible explanation and stop looking?
Explanation: Can I state my conclusion, justify the method I used to reach it, and present an argument that addresses the strongest objections — or can I only state the conclusion?
Self-Regulation: Have I genuinely examined my own reasoning for bias and motivated reasoning, or have I merely confirmed that my reasoning 'seems sound' from inside my own perspective?
seven_dispositions_self_assessment: Truth-Seeking: What is the most important piece of evidence that could prove my current position wrong? Have I looked for it?
Open-mindedness: Can I identify a position I currently hold that I would be most reluctant to change even with good evidence against it? Why is that?
Analyticity: Do I approach difficult problems with disciplined reasoning, or do I rely on intuition and hope it's right?
Systematicity: When working through a complex problem, do I maintain organized focus on the central question, or do I lose track of what I was trying to determine?
CT Self-Confidence: Have I held a position that the majority around me disagreed with — and maintained it because the evidence supported it, not because I was contrarian?
Inquisitiveness: When did I last pursue a question far beyond what was required because I genuinely wanted to understand?
Maturity of Judgment: Am I comfortable with the genuine uncertainty that serious inquiry often produces, or do I rush to conclude so I can feel resolved?

cctdi_and_cctst.description: The CCTDI (California Critical Thinking Dispositions Inventory) directly operationalizes the seven Delphi dispositions. The CCTST (California Critical Thinking Skills Test) directly operationalizes the six Delphi skills. Together these three form a coherent ecosystem: the Delphi Report provides the theoretical framework; the CCTST measures skill performance; the CCTDI measures dispositional orientation. Validity studies for both assessment instruments are conducted against the Delphi taxonomy.

paul_elder_framework.description: Paul and Elder's framework (Elements, Standards, Intellectual Virtues) and the Delphi framework both identify the same core requirements for CT but organize them differently. Delphi's six skills map to Paul-Elder's Elements of Thought (Interpretation ≈ Concepts + Purpose; Analysis ≈ Information + Assumptions; Evaluation ≈ Intellectual Standards; Inference ≈ Inference; Explanation ≈ Implications; Self-Regulation ≈ Intellectual Traits). Delphi's dispositions map to Paul-Elder's Intellectual Virtues.
paul_elder_framework.key_difference: Paul-Elder provides a more integrated, holistic model centered on the Elements of Thought as the unit of analysis; Delphi provides a more modular, independently-assessable skill taxonomy. Paul-Elder is better for deep thinking analysis; Delphi is better for granular skill assessment.

dewey_five_phases.description: Dewey's Five Phases describe the temporal structure of reflective thinking (how inquiry unfolds over time); the Delphi framework describes the cognitive skills required to carry out that inquiry (what capacities are required). The two frameworks are orthogonal but complementary: Interpretation and Analysis are most active in Dewey's Phases 1-3; Evaluation and Inference in Phases 3-4; Explanation and Self-Regulation in Phases 4-5.
dewey_five_phases.combined_use: Use Dewey's phases to understand where in an inquiry the student is; use Delphi skills to assess the quality of the cognitive work at each phase.

halpern_framework.relationship_type: Overlapping skill taxonomies from different disciplines
halpern_framework.description: Both Delphi and Halpern independently produced multi-skill CT taxonomies that converge substantially. Delphi emerged from philosophical consensus; Halpern from cognitive psychology research. Halpern's five skill categories (Verbal Reasoning, Argument Analysis, Hypothesis Testing, Likelihood, Decision Making) map onto subsets of Delphi's six skills. Delphi covers the explanation and self-regulation dimensions more explicitly; Halpern covers statistical reasoning and decision making more explicitly.
halpern_framework.complementarity: Use both: Delphi for a comprehensive canonical definition and skill taxonomy; Halpern for empirically-validated skill assessment (HCTA) and practical CT skill instruction with explicit transfer focus.
